title: Canada and the Allied Industrial Base
subtitle: What to secure, build, source from partners, and deploy

inlines.v: Canada's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as a resource and processing anchor: it ranks first among allies on

economies count it as their best-placed trusted partner somewhere in the chain. That role is allied before it is national: at home, uranium mining reads Watch, and battery and EV mineral mining, where Canada holds only

of world supply, read Partner. Its industrial effort should go into batteries, where it makes cells and packs, has committed investment in components and holds a supplier role in nickel chemicals. blocks.title: What Canada needs to deploy faster
blocks.alt: Bar chart of Canada's deployment need by technology, marking Accelerate and Watch and the main driver of each.

inlines.v: Deployment need by technology, with the largest of its measures: demand adequacy, the gap to national targets, or system need. Review cases, which rest on a single indicator of low confidence, are shown apart in grey and are not deployment priorities.

High deployment priority does not imply high manufacturing priority. The gas-turbine and LNG-plant Catch Ups are a separate capability call; the gas build-out itself should buy from whichever trusted supplier is ready. Storage, grid, wind and solar are worth watching, not forcing; a small renewables shortfall argues for a market footing, not local content. Clean hydrogen and oil use rest on a single indicator of low confidence, so both are review cases.

sections.title: Strategic agenda — what should Canada do next?

blocks.text: 1. Secure the rare-earth chain with allied partners

inlines.v: Build trusted separation, metal and magnet capacity with allies such as
Japan, Australia and the United States

through co-investment and offtake, and at home where a foothold can be built. Hold stocks sized to bridge the years until that supply qualifies, screen inbound investment in trusted capacity, and phase in limits on adversary sources in critical uses as it qualifies. No developing partner qualifies in this step; the AIB places new capacity in

blocks.text: 2. Keep cell and pack making competitive and catch up in battery components

inlines.v: Expand cell and pack production with finance for expansion, workforce and supplier development, tied to benchmarks, with the gate open to allied and conditional investment. In battery components, where
of imports, use time-limited production incentives and demand creation tied to benchmarks, at home and with allied partners.

blocks.text: 3. Build battery materials refining on the nickel chemicals base

inlines.v: Canada's anchor is its export share of refined battery materials, corroborated in nickel chemicals by a supplier role in the AIB. Tie production incentives, first-of-a-kind finance and workforce development to benchmarks, with sunsets, and keep the gate open to licensing and joint ventures that transfer capability in lithium, cathode and anode materials.

blocks.text: 4. Make mineral dependence deliberate and supplier roles reliable

inlines.v: Buy battery and EV minerals through offtake and co-investment with producers such as

, spread across several suppliers. Treat reliable supply of uranium, nickel chemicals and aluminium wire rod, and above all nuclear special materials, as an allied commitment, not a domestic fence. Source conversion and enrichment through co-investment and offtake with allied partners, such as

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate gas networks, keep sourcing open and narrow protection

inlines.v: Deploy gas networks faster through infrastructure, permitting and competitive procurement, with trusted-supplier conditions on public deployment support. Build storage, grid, wind and solar without local-content rules, and narrow protection on wafers and PV cells, grid metals refining and grid components, which are Watch steps.
Every number comes from the Country page data of the Allied Industrial Base Explorer (the data release of

) and from the Allied Industrial Base analysis. Each supply-chain step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order. A step is Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured, and a deployment step Accelerate where deployment need reaches
. A large, commoditized yard is Watch. Preserve needs a top-quarter Competitive Position (

). Catch Up needs high value, a lower position and a capability anchor corroborated by other evidence. Partner is high need with neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway; the rest is Watch.
Named layers, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice; a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
